speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This allows passengers to undergo both departure and arrival immigration clearance before boarding the train, and no further immigration clearance is required upon disembarkation in the other country.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Co-location of CIQ facilities for cross-border travel is not a novel arrangement and many other countries have this model.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For example, France and the United Kingdom (UK) have a longstanding similar arrangement for the Channel Tunnel, from which we took reference.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Even so, as this arrangement may be new to some Singaporeans, allow me to sketch out how the process will work for a typical traveller taking the RTS Link from Woodlands North Station in Singapore to Bukit Chagar Station in Malaysia.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: After going through the RTS Link fare gate at Woodlands North, the traveller will first undergo security checks and departure clearance by the Immigration and Checkpoints Authority (ICA) officers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The traveller will then proceed for arrival immigration clearance at Malaysia's CIQ zone at Woodlands North, which is located one level below ICA's departure clearance, in the same building.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Malaysia's officers will be deployed there to conduct immigration clearance and also conduct selective security checks.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: After arrival clearance, the traveller will go to the departure train platform and board the train to Bukit Chagar Station in Malaysia.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The traveller will not need to undergo further immigration clearance upon arrival in Malaysia and can just walk off the train straight into Johor Bahru.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Nevertheless, Malaysia's officers at Bukit Chagar Station may conduct further selective security checks, inspect customs permits, and collect taxes and duties, where necessary.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For travellers coming into Singapore, the immigration clearance process at Bukit Chagar Station in Malaysia will be identical, with travellers clearing both departure and arrival clearance at Bukit Chagar Station.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Through the co-located clearance arrangement, travellers will experience a more seamless and streamlined journey.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For this arrangement to work, each country will deploy its officers to the other country's territory to carry out the necessary CIQ functions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The approach for the Bill is for its provisions in the main body to have application to railways constructed under Singapore's Cross-Border Railways Act 2018 in general, and for the provisions pertaining to specific railways, like the RTS Link in this case, to be contained in Schedules.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The bilateral treaties and provisions specific to the RTS Link are listed in the First and Second Schedules respectively.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This allows our laws to accommodate future cross-border railways with a co-located model, should we come to such an arrangement in the future.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Bill, therefore, cannot be read in isolation and we must have regard to the arrangements contained in the Bilateral, as well as in the Supplementary Agreements.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In addition, in order to operationalise the co-located CIQ model, Malaysia must also pass domestic legislation to give effect to the arrangements that are set out in the bilateral treaties.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is because the arrangements are substantively mirrored for both countries.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In addition, reciprocity is a key principle which underpins the Bill's provisions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The privileges and protections that the Bill accords to Malaysia's officers deployed in Singapore are, by design, contingent upon the privileges and protections which Malaysia's legislation accords to Singapore officers deployed in Malaysia.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Malaysia's legislation for the RTS Link passed both Chambers of its Parliament earlier this year and provides for these reciprocal privileges and protections.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The provisions of the Bill, Sir, cover four broad areas.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: First, co-located border control functions, in both Singapore and Malaysia.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Second, cross-border incident management, including the establishment of concurrent criminal jurisdiction on board trains in transit between both countries.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Third, other matters, such as data protection, as well as protection and immunities for Malaysia's officers deployed in Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Fourth, related and consequential amendments to other Acts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I will start with the co-located border control functions in Singapore, addressed in Parts 2 and 3 of the Bill.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: First, the Bill circumscribes the areas in Singapore within which Malaysia's officers can perform their CIQ duties.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For the RTS Link, these designated areas lie within the Woodlands North Station.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Clause 7 empowers the Minister for Home Affairs to demarcate the designated areas.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Clear signages will be displayed at all designated areas at the Woodlands North Station to ensure that the public is aware of the perimeter of these areas.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: To be clear, there is no change to territorial boundaries and the designated areas for Malaysia remain Singapore's territory and subject to Singapore's laws.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Clause 8 makes clear that Singapore law continues to apply within the designated areas.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The list of Malaysian laws which would be allowed to apply within the designated areas are strictly for CIQ clearance and security checks, and these are contained in paragraph 16 of the Second Schedule.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Second, the Bill empowers the Minister to approve which Malaysian officers may be deployed in Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Clause 9 states that only officers whom the Minister recognises as Malaysian preclearance officers in relation to a cross-border railway are allowed to be deployed in Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Under exceptional circumstances, such as a massive outage or, perhaps, a public health emergency, Malaysia might need to deploy additional manpower in the designated areas in Singapore at short notice.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Clause 10 allows for such expeditious deployments for a limited period, provided the Malaysian Government gives written notice under this provision.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Third, the Bill authorises the calibrated exercise of powers by Malaysia's officers within the designated areas in Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Clauses 4 and 5 provide a list of "ordinary", or routine, powers required for the conduct of CIQ duties in the context of a cross-border railway.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These include requiring individuals to present travel and import documents, screening checks, such as requiring travellers to put their bags through scanners, and so on.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Clause 13 states that Malaysia's officers are authorised to conduct border clearance and railway security checks to the extent conferred by Malaysian border control laws.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Their exercise of powers is subject to limits set out in clauses 14 to 18.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This spells out the specific legal powers that Malaysia's officers can exercise within the designated areas and the scope of its application.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: When an individual is detained, Malaysia's officers must, as soon as is practicable, transfer custody of the person to an appropriate Singapore officer.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Fourth, the Bill empowers Singapore officers to check for items that are controlled or prohibited under Malaysian law.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is catered for to streamline the conduct of checks between Singapore and Malaysia under the co-located clearance model.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Clause 19 enables Singapore officers to check for such items, even if they are not prohibited or controlled under Singapore law.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Malaysian officers at Bukit Chagar station are similarly empowered by Malaysia's legislation to check for items prohibited or controlled under Singapore law.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: There will, however, be exceptions, such as where an item poses a threat to human safety, is a live creature or constitutes evidential material relevant to an investigation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Then in such cases, the item must be removed from the traveller or taken possession of by Singapore officers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And that is the focus of Part 4 of the Bill.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Clause 22 states that, as a precondition for sending Singapore officers to Malaysia, the Minister must be satisfied that Malaysian law allows Singapore officers to conduct their official duties in Malaysia properly, under the orders of their own commanding officers and that they are conferred with the powers, duties and privileges of their counterparts in Malaysia.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is in addition to the protections and immunities that Malaysia's legislation accords to Singapore officers deployed to Malaysia.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Clause 24 makes clear that every Singapore officer deployed to Malaysia in relation to cross-border railways has the same powers, rights and immunities as they do when performing the same duties in Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The clause also provides the limits to the exercise of powers by Malaysia's officers in Singapore apply similarly to the exercise of powers by our officers in Malaysia.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This means, for example, that Singapore officers are not allowed to make an arrest when in Malaysia's territory.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Clause 25 provides for prescribed Singapore border control laws to apply within Singapore's designated areas in Malaysia, to empower our officers to carry out border clearance and security checks.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The list of Singapore border control laws applicable for the RTS Link is set out in paragraph 17 of the Second Schedule.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This will ensure that the level of checks done is comparable to that at our other checkpoints and that there will be no compromise to our border security.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Besides checkpoint operations, we must also be prepared for contingencies that may occur on a moving train.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Safety and security incidents may occur from time to time, due to technical faults or as a result of sabotage, resulting in trains stopping mid-way during the trip.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Officers from both countries may then be required to respond, even if the incident occurs within the other country's territory.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For this reason, the Bill includes provisions for managing incidents that occur on the railway tracks or on trains moving between the countries, or what we call "trains in transit", for short.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The codification in law provides legal certainty for the officers who will be called upon to respond.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Beyond the Bill's provisions, Singapore and Malaysia have also developed detailed protocols and standard operating procedures to facilitate timely and coordinated responses to such cross-border incidents on the RTS Link.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Officers will be trained and empowered to keep travellers safe and secure.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Both countries will hold joint exercises prior to the commencement of the operationalisation of the revenue service, and on a regular basis thereafter, to ensure continued operational readiness.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These principles form the basis of paragraph 14 of the Second Schedule: First, where a train is able to complete its journey, any incident on board will be managed by the authorities of the country in which the train stops.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Second, if a train stalls and is unable to complete its journey, the country in whose territory the train is situated will manage the incident.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The country with primary responsibility will be the Incident Manager in this case and will have command and control over incident management.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, in the case of a train bound for Singapore, so long as the nose of the train has not crossed Pier 48, Malaysia will be the Incident Manager.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: However, once the nose has crossed Pier 48, Singapore will be the Incident Manager.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And this is so even if most of the train's length remains otherwise within Malaysia's territory.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For a Malaysia-bound train, so long as the nose has not crossed Pier 47, Singapore will be the Incident Manager.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Once the nose has crossed Pier 47, Malaysia will be the Incident Manager, and in similar terms, even if most of the train's length remains within Singapore's territory.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Fourth, in the absence of a train, for incidents occurring on the railway tracks between Piers 47 and 48, the country whose officers arrive on the scene first will be the Incident Manager.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, there might be a scenario where you might have persons on the track where there is no train and in such a case, the country whose officers arrive first will take control of the situation and will be designated the Incident Manager.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Fifth, for all cross-border incidents, when one country has assumed the role of Incident Manager, the other country shall render the necessary support upon request.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Last, to ensure coordinated response, when each country's officers need to cross the administrative boundary marker of the other country during incident management, they must obtain prior consent of the other country before doing so.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: However, if the incident is determined to be a search and rescue operation or a medical evacuation, then each country's officers need only inform the other country before crossing over.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Part 5 of the Bill sets out the scope, duties and powers for officers managing cross-border incidents.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Under clause 29, cross-border incident management operations will be limited to the premises where an incident has occurred and its immediate vicinity, as is reasonably necessary for an effective response.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Clause 28 empowers our officers to carry out cross-border incident management duties within the locations prescribed by clause 29, including in Malaysia's territory, if necessary.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It also allows Malaysia's officers to carry out equivalent duties in Singapore's territory, if necessary.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Clause 27 spells out the scope of these duties.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These include the protection of people from injury or death, and the protection of public property from damage or loss, whether arising from criminal acts or in any other way.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Paragraph 15 of the Second Schedule further sets out the range of powers that Malaysia's officers are allowed to exercise in Singapore's territory for the purpose of cross-border incident management at the RTS Link, and makes clear that these must be exercised with reasonable force.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Apart from major cross-border incidents, we must also consider routine crimes that may take place on board RTS Link trains, such as theft or perhaps, outrage of modesty.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Otherwise, the respective country in whose territory the offence happens will have criminal jurisdiction.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Clause 39 under Part 7 of the Bill establishes Singapore's jurisdiction over criminal offences on board trains in transit in the general context of cross-border railways, including when the train is in Malaysia's territory and at certain defined zones of the railway tracks.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This then enables Singapore to investigate and prosecute offences committed at these locations, even if they might be outside Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Malaysia, through its legislation, has also established jurisdiction over criminal offences on board trains in transit and on the railway tracks between Piers 47 and 48.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Singapore has worked out with Malaysia a method for determining which country has primary right to exercise jurisdiction in any given case.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In coming up with this principle, we took reference from the arrangement between the UK and France at the Channel Tunnel.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is also similar to the approach taken towards investigating offences on board airborne aircraft, where the destination country has primary right.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It therefore does not matter whether travellers file a Police report in Singapore or in Malaysia.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We also have a referral system in place: if a country receives a report for which it does not have primary right to exercise jurisdiction, it will refer the case to the other country.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Should the country without primary right wish to conduct investigations into the matter, it may request for the other country to waive its right.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This framework ensures clarity of jurisdiction when the exact location of the offence is unclear.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It also allows Singapore to investigate offences where there is public interest to do so.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Bill also addresses other matters, such as those concerning data protection, as well as protection and immunities for Malaysia's officers in Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: With both countries' CIQ facilities co-located in both stations, data protection is a key consideration, and this is the subject of Part 6 of the Bill.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Clause 38 provides that documents, devices and equipment belonging to the Singapore Government shall be immune from seizure, confiscation or any other form of interference when installed, kept or situated within defined areas in Malaysia.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The protection of Singapore's data and the inviolability of our documents, devices and equipment have been provided for in Malaysia's legislation as well.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: On a reciprocal basis, clause 35 of the Bill provides for the protection of information and data collected or generated by Malaysia's officers in Singapore, in the course of official duties.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And similarly, clause 36 provides for the inviolability of documents, devices and equipment belonging to the Malaysian government when installed, kept or situated within defined areas in Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Part 8 of the Bill confers protection on Malaysia's officers deployed in Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This extends to Malaysia's officers the same level of protection against abuse as Singapore's public servants, in the course of their conducting official duties.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In addition, clause 43 confers immunity on the actions of Malaysia's officers in Singapore from Singapore's criminal, civil and administrative jurisdictions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is provided those actions are committed in the course of official duties.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Malaysian government may waive this immunity at its discretion.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is our commitment to our own officers, who work tirelessly to safeguard Singapore's borders.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: First, amendments are proposed for the purpose of adapting existing laws to the requirements of a cross-border railway.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For example, clause 63 amends section 5 of the Immigration Act to empower the Minister to prescribe an area outside Singapore as an authorised point of entry or immigration control post.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For the RTS Link, Singapore's designated areas at Bukit Chagar station will be prescribed as an authorised point of entry.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Another example is clause 51, which amends section 24 of the Coroners Act, so that coronial jurisdiction may be asserted in cases where a death occurs on a train in transit, even if outside Singapore, if the body is transported into Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This allows Singapore to investigate cases of unnatural death that have been reported, where there is public interest to do so.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Second, amendments are proposed for the purpose of allowing the deployment of Singapore officers to Malaysian territory to perform official duties.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Clauses 48, 65 and 70 amend the Civil Defence Act, the Immigration Act and the Police Force Act respectively.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These amendments empower the Minister to send the Singapore Civil Defence Force (SCDF), ICA and the Singapore Police Force (SPF) officers to Malaysia for the purpose of performing official duties in relation to cross-border railways, including for cross-border incident management.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These are largely offences under Singapore's immigration laws.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The RTS Link will significantly transform the way commuters move between the two countries, and I believe improve the lives of hundreds of thousands of people who cross the Singapore-Malaysia border every day.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Many commuters may spend hours each day in traffic congestion.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is time that could otherwise be spent at work, with family, or at rest.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It also imposes a mental and physical toll on commuters, who must cope daily with uncertainty and long waiting times at checkpoints.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This should significantly reduce congestion at checkpoints and shorten travel times.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It will also provide greater comfort and predictability for commuters, which is particularly important for those who rely on cross-border travel for their livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Singapore is well positioned to implement such seamless clearance arrangements.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Our ICA has already deployed advanced automated clearance systems across our land, sea and air checkpoints.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Many travellers today are familiar with biometric clearance lanes, which use facial recognition, iris scans and fingerprints to very quickly identify individuals and have them clear customs.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These systems have proven to be efficient and secure.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: They allow us to process large volumes of travellers while maintaining high standards of border security.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Malaysia, too, has been investing in similar technologies.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These developments give confidence that both countries have the technical capability and operational experience to support a smooth clearance process for RTS Link passengers, without compromising on safety or security standards.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: First, on the purpose of allowing Malaysian border controls to be applied within Singapore.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Bill provides for Malaysian officers to exercise powers under Malaysian border control laws within a designated area in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: At the same time, it makes clear that Singapore law continues to apply within that area.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think it would be helpful for the Minister to perhaps elaborate on why it is necessary for Malaysian law to have application within Singapore territory, rather than relying purely on Singapore law with the appropriate cooperation mechanisms?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And also, if there are potential conflicts between Singapore law and Malaysian law on a particular issue, how will that be managed in practice?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Second, on the extent of powers that Malaysian officers may exercise while in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Bill sets out a framework under which Malaysian officers may conduct border clearance and security checks within the designated area.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: At the same time, it imposes certain limits.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For example, Malaysian officers are not permitted to make arrests in Singapore, and any detained persons or seized items must be transferred to Singapore authorities within a reasonable time.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Could the Minister clarify how will accountability and oversight be ensured for actions taken by foreign officers operating in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In addition, what avenues of recourse will be available to individuals who may have complaints about the conduct of such officers and how will these be investigated and resolved across jurisdictions?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Third, on the handling of routine crimes on board cross-border trains.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think the Minister has clarified exactly which laws will apply – and it appears that where train is stopped, it will be between Piers 47 and 48, the nose of the train that will define which law applies; and on a moving train it will be the destination country's laws that apply.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, I think these are helpful clarifications and my only further questions are, operationally, will joint patrols or onboard security personnel be deployed in the trains?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And if so, which countries will do this?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And will those officers have the relevant authority to take action if and when an incident occurs even if it happens to be in the other territory?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Given that the travel time is only about five minutes, it may not be easy to ascertain exactly where an incident occurs and will be important for whichever officer is present to have the authority to deal with an incident, as and when it rises.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Fourth, on the coordination in the event of cross-border incidents.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Bill provides provisions for incident management operations, including the ability of officers – so this was the point I mentioned earlier, operating with the other.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think this is sensible, but it will be good to know exactly what the boundaries are for these officers.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I will also be interested if the Minister can elaborate on how command and control will operate during such incidents?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Who will have overall authority of an incident, and how will responsibilities be allocated between Singapore and Malaysian officers?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, say, for example, a train has a destination in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Malaysian officers spot the incident, who will that Malaysian officer report to and how will the incident be dealt with?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Also, will there be joint exercises conducted ahead of the RTS Link opening to ensure that both sides are well prepared to respond swiftly and cohesively, and any command-and-control issues will be dealt with easily as well.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Can the Minister provide more details on how these measures will be implemented operationally?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The co-location of border controls necessarily involves a degree of legal and operational integration between two sovereign countries.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It requires mutual trust, clear rules and strong safeguards to ensure that both security and sovereignty are preserved.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In this regard, I think the Bill strikes a good balance.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As we move towards opening the RTS Link, it is important that both countries get these arrangements right.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Done well, this will not only ease congestion and improve the lives of both Singaporeans and Malaysians, but also strengthen the close economic and social ties between Singapore and Malaysia.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In developing this framework, I believe that the Ministry has looked towards international models like the Channel Tunnel between the UK and France.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The 1986 Treaty of Canterbury taught us that for a cross-border rail to succeed, sovereignty must be expressed through clear control zones rather than rigid physical borders.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While the Workers' Party supports the principles of efficiency and bilateral cooperation underpinning this Bill, I have several clarifications regarding legal jurisdiction, officer protection and commuter rights.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The Ministry has stated that Malaysian officers who detain an individual must hand them over to Singapore officers as soon as is practicable.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In the Channel Tunnel context, delays in these handovers occasionally led to legal challenges regarding the lawfulness of detention.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In a facility designed for 10,000 passengers per hour, practicable is a subjective term.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: So, what is the physical and operational infrastructure in place at Woodlands North to ensure this transfer happens immediately or as soon as practicable?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Will there be a permanent co-located Singapore Police force presence within the Malaysian designated area to ensure there is zero dead time between detention and handover?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The Channel Tunnel model uses a primary jurisdiction rule to avoid confusion, yet it leaves room for the home country to step in for their own citizens.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We must also ensure a transparent mechanism exists to update victims' families if a case is handed over to foreign authorities.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The RTS Link involves a 25-metre-high marine viaduct across the Straits of Johor.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Learning from the 1996 Euro Tunnel fire, we know that seconds are lost if emergency responders face jurisdictional paralysis.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Under Part 5 of this Bill, how will the division of labour between the SCDF and the Jabatan Bomba dan Penyelamat Malaysia be managed and permitted under the bill during a mid-track emergency?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Will there be a single unified incident commander to prevent confusion on the viaduct, and how frequently will joint tabletop exercises be mandated by law?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: With a heavy reliance on automated e-gates and QR code clearance.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We must not overlook vulnerable commuters within the Malaysian designated area at Woodlands North.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Will there be a guaranteed minimum quota of manual counters staffed by Singapore officers?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This is essential for our seniors and persons with disabilities who may struggle with automated systems in a high-pressure environment.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Indeed, for this arrangement to be truly reciprocal, our officers at Bukit Chagar must have the same operational autonomy and protection as the Malaysian officers have in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In its media release, MHA also referred to the Channel Fixed Link.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: A point of friction in the Channel Tunnel model was the disparity in the powers granted to officers operating in the other's territory.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I understand that under the Sangatte Protocol, British officers on French soil lacked equivalent powers to domestic law enforcement and could not execute independent arrest, which led to persistent ambiguity regarding the use of force, such as applying restraints, pending French police's intervention.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Given that MHA has explicitly looked to the Channel Tunnel model for the RTS Link framework, I wonder whether the Ministry has studied the relevance of their operational experience to our RTS Link, and if it is relevant, whether expected similar operational gaps have been or will be addressed.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: MHA has noted that Singapore-issued equipment at Bukit Chagar will be inviolable.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While the hardware is protected, I seek clarity on the digital data.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Will the data collected by our officers in Johor be transmitted via a dedicated air-gapped network back to Singapore to prevent any potential interception vulnerabilities, while operating on foreign soil?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The Minister reserves the power to revoke the recognition of Malaysian officer without giving a reason.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While I understand the security necessity, may I ask if there is a predefined framework of red flags agreed upon with our counterparts?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Maintaining a stable professional relationship between both border forces is critical to preventing operational friction.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The Cross-Border Railways (Border Control Co-location) Bill currently before this House is intended to provide the legal framework for this significant project.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The Government has drawn reference from the Channel Tunnel model between the UK and France, where co-location arrangements have improved immigration clearance efficiency.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: That said, I wish to seek clarification on several legal and operational details.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We must ensure that the families of victims receive transparent and timely updates.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Will there be a unified incident commander to prevent confusion during critical moments of a rescue operation?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While automated clearance gates and QR codes are now widely used, many elderly persons and individuals with disabilities may encounter difficulties with these systems.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I hope the Government can assure this House that sufficient manned counters will be retained within the Malaysian clearance zone at Woodlands North Station.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Fifth, legal protections for officers and data security.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Furthermore, will the immigration data collected onsite be transmitted back to Singapore via an independent encrypted network to guard against data breaches?

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: And with such heavy traffic, definitely, something is going to happen, incidents of any nature.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: I wish to address some critical areas for discussion.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: And if they are allowed to carry firearms, how is it being governed in terms of jurisdiction?

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Because, if you move from one, let us say, leave the Woodlands North Station, which is towards Johor, then basically, by the point of destination, then actually, we do not have jurisdiction on board.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: So, how do we address that and vice versa for the Malaysians?

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Third, when our security reach the Johor station, how does the security transit to the return trip because then, they will be carrying firearms, if that is the intention?

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: So, I think all these need to be addressed carefully.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: But I think this scenario is good for discussion.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: In the case of, let us say, an "emergency brake" situation.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Let us say a train leaves Bukit Chagar Station towards Singapore's Woodlands North Station, the destination on board is under Singapore jurisdiction.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: However, before we reach Pier 47, that means at Pier 48, there is an emergency brake and maybe, there is an incident on board and our security takes action.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: If the passengers do not disembark and the train carries on, then I think it is in Singapore's jurisdiction.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: But if, let us say, the train is being towed back to Bukit Chagar, then what will happen?

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: So, those are the scenarios that are possible that we have to think through.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Maybe we have to do dry runs on it to resolve it.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Having personally taken the Eurostar train from the UK to continental Europe, I have experienced how the co-location of British and French border Police at the St Pancras station in London saved time for passengers entering Europe by rail.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Similarly, to ease travel between Singapore and Malaysia, this Bill to co-locate border controls should be supported.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: My party colleague Dennis Tan has asked for clarifications on various aspects of the Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On my part, I wish to make brief observations on Part 7 of the Bill dealing with criminal jurisdiction.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is reflected in clause 39(1) of the Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As both countries could potentially exercise jurisdiction over crimes committed in these locations, the Ministry states that there are arrangements on which country has precedence.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It has explained that, in general, the country in whose territory the train journey is completed has the primary right to exercise jurisdiction.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Earlier, the Minister confirmed this in his Second Reading speech.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Thus, if the journey is completed in Johor, Malaysia would have primary jurisdiction, and vice versa, if the journey is completed in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These arrangements mentioned in the media release are not reflected in the language of Part 7 of the Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In contrast, the Malaysian law on this matter is more explicit.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Ministry's media release goes on to state that the country with primary jurisdiction may waive its right if there is a request by the other country to take over the case on the ground that there is greater public interest for the requesting country to investigate and prosecute.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We are thus given to understand that there would be situations where, even though the train was travelling to Singapore, Singapore may give up its primary jurisdiction to Malaysia.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: When Singapore may give up its primary jurisdiction to Malaysia is found in clause 39(2) of the Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, the person must be subject to the criminal jurisdiction of the country the conduct was engaged in, in this case, Malaysia.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Second, Malaysia must not be subject to any obligation to cede jurisdiction to Singapore.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: And third, Malaysia must have brought criminal proceedings.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If my understanding is correct, when all these three conditions are met, Singapore cannot prosecute the offender, even if the conduct occurred on a trip completed at Woodlands.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Under what circumstances would Malaysia be obligated to cede jurisdiction to Singapore?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Could the Minister please clarify where these obligations are from and in what situations would they arise?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Additionally, I note that the Bills of both countries do not mention an important consideration highlighted in MHA's media release – that one country may waive its jurisdiction at the request of the other if there is greater public interest for the requesting country to investigate and prosecute.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Perhaps, the omission is because it is difficult to codify how a greater public interest should be assessed.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Nonetheless, there will be cases whereby both countries have real stakes in curbing the criminal activity and be equally interested to handle the case.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For example, someone who is bringing controlled drugs from Malaysia to Singapore through the RTS Link would be simultaneously committing offences under the laws of both countries.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Who will determine whether there is greater public interest for Malaysia to prosecute, and how would this determination be made?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In that regard, I would like to make an observation about potential bilateral sensitivities that may arise.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: From my brief research into Malaysian law, it is clear that while we share a colonial heritage and had similar laws at one time, the criminal laws of our two countries have evolved to show significant differences.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For example, while the offence of theft in both countries is still criminalised under section 379 of the Penal Code of both countries, the punishment for theft in Singapore carries a maximum of three years, while in Malaysia, the maximum jail term is up to seven years.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This could be for various reasons, such as the differences in law and punishments or to give their nationals better access to justice in their home countries.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I personally do not think we need to harmonise the laws of both countries as each country is sovereign, has its own priorities and determines its own laws.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Nevertheless, it would be useful to know if the Ministry foresees that such bilateral tensions may arise and whether there are any protocols in place to manage them.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This Bill deals with the technical aspects of jurisdiction and law, yet it has very practical impact for the everyday commuter seeking to cross the border; shaping the way immigration is experienced at the checkpoints.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: For the commuter, the questions are straightforward: when I make this journey, do I understand what rules apply, and can I rely on them being applied clearly and consistently?

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: When Singaporeans tap in at Woodlands North, are they already subject to Malaysian law?

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: If Singaporeans unknowingly carry something that is not allowed into Malaysia, will they be stopped on our side?

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: If an incident happens mid-journey, who investigates and under which law?

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: If there is an accident, a dispute, a lost item or even a medical emergency on the train, which country’s officers should we approach for help?

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I support the Bill and I would like to seek clarification on several aspects of the Bill hoping to cover some of the practical concerns that commuters may have arising from the Bill.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: But each of these systems is shaped by its own legal and bilateral context.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: So, my first question is this: how does our framework differ from those models and what were the specific design choices made for Singapore and Malaysia?

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Understanding this will help us better appreciate the safeguards embedded in our system and whether there are lessons we have consciously adopted or chosen to depart from.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The Bill also envisages multiple zones as a commuter moves across the border: the designated areas, the defined zone and the train in transit.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Across these zones, laws may shift or apply concurrently.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: From a commuter's perspective, this raises a practical question: at what point do Malaysian cross-border laws apply within the Malaysia designated areas located in Singapore and how does this interact with the continued application of Singapore law?

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: For example, where a traveller carries an item that is unregulated in Singapore but regulated under Malaysian law will the traveller be stopped within the Malaysia designated area located in Singapore?

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Will there be an opportunity to dispose of the item?

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Will differences in the laws that apply have any practical impact on commuters, of course, beyond what is already encountered at conventional checkpoints and how will these situations be managed operationally?

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This leads me to my next point on concurrent criminal jurisdiction.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Matters such as public disorder, voluntarily causing hurt, molestation and drug‑related offences in transit areas are not hypothetical concerns; they will need to be dealt with if and when they arise.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I therefore wish to seek clarity on the precise circumstances and locations in which concurrent criminal jurisdiction is contemplated under the Bill and on the mechanisms by which competing jurisdiction is intended to be managed.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: First, where the same conduct is an offence under both Singapore and Malaysian law, and both countries have jurisdiction, how will it be decided which side will take the lead in the prosecution?

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The Minister earlier mentioned that the country for which the train is bound will take the lead.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: For example, what if there is a disagreement on the proviso under clause 39(2)?

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: If Singapore disagrees that there is no obligation to cede jurisdiction, for example?

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Second, on clause 40, could the Minister clarify how the Public Prosecutor's consent mechanism will operate in practice?

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: More broadly, how will this safeguard ensure that individuals are not exposed to the risk of double prosecution for the same conduct?

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: My next point relates to enforcement powers of preclearance officers.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Clauses 15 and 18 make clear that the Malaysian preclearance officers in Singapore may remove items or detain individuals for the purposes of border control but they must transfer the custody to Singapore officers, and they do not have arrest powers.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: If the Malaysian authorities intend to assume custody of the items or the individual, how will this be carried out?

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Will this be done through existing legal frameworks such as mutual legal assistance, operational cooperation or extradition processes?

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Once the individual or item is in custody with Singapore authorities, will the case then proceed fully under Singapore's evidence laws and the criminal procedure?

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Clause 24 is a mirror provision in that it provides the same limits on the powers of a Singapore preclearance officer in the Singapore designated area in Malaysia.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: On this note, how would Singapore criminal law apply in the designated area?

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Such conduct can be prosecuted and punished by Singapore Courts, regardless of whether it is an offence under Malaysian laws.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: However, Singapore officers cannot arrest the person for that conduct until the person is physically within Singapore.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: My next point relates to the powers, privileges and immunities of the officers.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Clause 43 provides certain immunities to the Malaysian preclearance and incident management officers in the discharge of their duties.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Could the Minister clarify what happens if those powers are exceeded?

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: What channels of redress are available to affected individuals?

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: And how will it assess whether the duties, powers and protections are, in law or in practice, substantially less favourable?

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I am heartened that the Bill expressly addresses cross-border incidents, including security, public order and medical emergencies within the transit areas.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: There is a considered and well-structured approach in doing this.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: But I would like to seek clarification on the operational aspects.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: For example, in the event of a train breakdown in transit, how will repairs, recovery or towing be handled?

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Will these arrangements be set out in subsidiary legislation, bilateral agreements, or operator-level protocols?

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: How will we ensure that the experience of the traveller continues to be of good quality?

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Second, on major incidents, where an incident extends beyond defined zones or requires coordinated response from both sides, how will the coordination be carried out in practice?

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: What are the protocols for joint operations, and how will command and responsibility be determined in such situations?

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: How will this impact response times to these major incidents?

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Much will depend on the ability of our officers on the ground to deal with the matters or seek or grant consent quickly.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Clarity on these operational points will be important to ensure the framework works effectively on the ground.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: How will such data be stored, processed and transmitted back to Singapore?

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: What safeguards including infrastructural guardrails are in place to prevent unauthorised access or breaches?

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: In the event of a data breach, what avenues of accountability and redress will there be?

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I will conclude on a brief point on operational readiness.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: It supports a more efficient approach to cross-border movement between Singapore and Malaysia.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Much will depend on how these arrangements are implemented on the ground.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Officers will need to be clear on the scope of their powers, the limits of their authority and the zones within which they operate.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: And information must be handled securely and responsibly.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is part of how families manage their time, how workers earn their livelihoods and how businesses stay connected.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I have spoken to residents who make it.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I have heard the stories of parents, workers and small business owners who depend on it.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Johor Bahru-Singapore RTS Link promises to transform this experience.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It promises to turn what is today sometimes a long commute into a seamless transit.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I support this Bill because for the RTS Link to succeed, the border clearance process must be as efficient as the journey itself.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But a border made seamless for convenience must never become invisible for accountability.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, accountability and sovereignty in practice.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: So, I ask: how is an ordinary resident able to distinguish between a legitimate official act and an abuse of power that results in harm?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And if that line is crossed, who determines that?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Where such powers are exercised, accountability must be real and accessible.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If a Singaporean suffers harm or has their data mishandled, what is their practical recourse?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will they be expected to navigate a foreign legal system?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For residents, this is not about legal theory.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is about whether help is real, accessible and within reach when something goes wrong.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I acknowledge that, in law, an officer acting outside the proper discharge of duty may not be protected by immunity.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But for residents, the question is whether there is a clear and workable path to seek redress.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If something goes wrong on our soil, people must know where to turn to and who will answer.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will the Government consider a dedicated liaison mechanism to assist Singaporeans and visitors in navigating these cross-border issues?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Our officers will operate in Malaysia under similar arrangements.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What support will they receive if they face disputes or accusations while carrying out their duties?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Clause 44 allows the Minister to act if reciprocity fails.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I also seek clarification on the practical limits of these arrangements.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While Malaysian officers exercise powers within designated areas, can the Government clarify how Singapore law applies if they step outside these areas in a personal capacity?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Similarly, if offences, such as bribery or misconduct, occur within the Malaysia designated area in Singapore, can Singapore authorities investigate and take action where conduct falls outside official duties?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: On Singapore soil, accountability cannot stop at the boundary line of a designated area.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, Mr Deputy Speaker Sir, the privacy and dignity of travellers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Explanatory Statement suggests that strip and body searches require consent.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Yet, the Second Schedule allows such searches in certain situations.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Government clarify the thresholds clearly, particularly when non-consensual searches may be carried out based on reasonable suspicion?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Security must be firm, but it must also be understood.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Malaysian officers may detain individuals and use reasonable force.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: To be clear, they cannot make arrests in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They must transfer custody to Singapore officers as soon as reasonably practicable.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The issue is whether safeguards are consistently applied.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Under section 16, questioning can take place without a Singapore officer present.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Clause 15 requires detainees to be handed over without undue delay.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will the Ministry provide clear, public-facing guidelines so that travellers understand both their rights and the limits of these powers?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Trust is built not just on what powers exist, but on how clearly they are explained and how fairly they are exercised.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Third, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, incident response and safety.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Clause 28 allows officers to operate across borders.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But in the first critical minutes, who is in charge?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Clause 32 allows incident management officers to bear arms, subject to legal limits.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Minister clarify the rules governing the use of firearms and how accountability will be ensured if force is used?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will criminal jurisdiction under section 39 interact with immunity provisions under section 43?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: When force is used, there must be no doubt about the answers and under which law.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: On clause 10, deemed recognition allows additional officers during serious incidents.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will victims and their families know which country takes the lead in the investigation?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If a serious offence, such as drug trafficking, occurs within the Malaysian designated area in Singapore, which law applies?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If an offence occurs in the Singapore designated area in Malaysia, when does Singapore law take effect?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For offences committed in transit, how will section 39 be applied?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Designated areas must not become legal grey zones when enforcement becomes uncertain.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The parent planning the day around the crossing.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I support making movement faster and more predictable.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But I have also raised important clarifications on accountability, dignity, crisis response and the application of the law.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Because this Bill does not operate in isolation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: When the border becomes faster, decisions become faster.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We are already in a period of global uncertainty.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: When the border becomes easier to cross, spending becomes easier to shift.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is why we must look beyond convenience.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must ask how local demand will evolve.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Connectivity creates opportunity but it also creates competition.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: So, the question is not whether we should build this link.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Because in uncertain times, convenience alone is not enough.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And if we get this right, we will not only build a more efficient crossing.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We will build a system that is fair, trusted and resilient.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As some Members have noted, I have already covered some of the points in my opening speech, so I do not propose to repeat them, but nonetheless, there are quite a number of process questions which I thought I will just take in turn.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Vikram Nair, Ms Cassandra Lee and Mr Yip Hon Weng asked about the implications arising from the application of Malaysian laws at Woodlands North Station.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is an important point, so, let me just take some time to clarify this.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These designated areas will be clearly demarcated with signages, as required by clause 7 of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: LTA will work closely with its Malaysian counterparts to ensure that there is clarity and there are sufficient signages, and that they are prominently displayed and presented in our official languages.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Second, I had mentioned that the application of Malaysia's border control laws in the designated areas in Woodlands North Station is for the sole purpose of empowering the Malaysian officers to conduct the necessary border clearances and security checks on travellers departing for Malaysia.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Members might recall that it is because they have their border control located within Singapore, so we need to give them legal effect for them to do the work that they do to clear, so that we also have a corresponding arrangement on the Bukit Chagar side.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The effect of applying these laws in the designated areas would be similar to what travellers would encounter at the usual checkpoints in Malaysia when travelling to Malaysia.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, the experience is not altogether dissimilar, it is just that we put these powers and the framework into the checkpoint at Woodlands North Station and correspondingly, on the other side, Bukit Chagar.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As I mentioned earlier, the list of Malaysian laws that would apply in the designated areas is set out in paragraph 16 of the Second Schedule.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Without these laws in place in the framework that we have proposed in this Bill, in the designated areas in Woodlands North Station, Malaysian officers, who operate here, would have no legal backing to carry out their duties here, and then, in that respect, the co-located CIQ model would not work.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Clause 8 of this Bill makes this point clear.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Singapore law remains in effect over the entirety of Woodlands North Station, even within the designated areas.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Singapore officers are available to assist travellers if needed.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If travellers encounter issues or need help in the designated areas, they should act similar to how they would anywhere else in Singapore and where necessary, seek help from Singapore authorities.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Vikram, Ms Lee and Mr Yip also asked about the recourse available if Malaysia's officers operating in Singapore exceed the scope of what they are allowed to do.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Bill sets clear limits to the powers that the Malaysian officers have when they exercise their duties in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For example, on the power to take possession of dangerous or controlled items uncovered during checks and detain individuals in connection with the above, clause 15 provides that Malaysian preclearance officers transfer custody of these items or individuals to a Singapore officer as soon as is practicable.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Do not forget, they are located in the same space, in the same checkpoint, in both Bukit Chagar as well as in Woodlands North Station.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This means that if a Malaysian officer detects such items, he is required to contact ICA officers without undue delay, for ICA officers to then deal with in accordance with our domestic standard operating procedures and in accordance with Singapore law.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They are contingent on those actions being undertaken as part of their official duties in the designated areas.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Actions taken outside of that or which exceed the scope of these duties would then not be protected by the immunities.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We want to have the flexibility and ability to determine, on a case-by-case basis, and depending on what the facts might present at that location, whether we need to exercise this power.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I should make clear, for completeness, that we should distinguish the powers set out under the main provisions of the Bill and those under the Second Schedule.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There might have been some conflation and so, I thought I will take some time to explain this.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The main body of the Bill is focused on what I called earlier, the "ordinary" powers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These are the baseline powers that are necessary for the day-to-day work of conducting border clearance and security checks.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These include the powers to require travellers to present their passport, refuse entry of persons or goods and perform screening and other searches, such as body searches.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These are powers that are already provided to our own officers today for routine border clearance and security checks.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Second Schedule, however, contains "special" powers, or what I called "special" powers in my speech earlier.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These are the powers that equip officers with the legal basis to manage non-routine situations and ensure travellers' safety and security.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They are also no different from the powers that ICA officers already have today for managing incidents at the existing checkpoints.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These powers have been codified in the bilateral RTS Link Supplementary Agreement entered into with Malaysia.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The circumstances in which these powers will be used are limited.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For example, officers are allowed to use reasonable force for purposes of detaining an individual who behaves in a disorderly or threatening manner.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And to Mr Yip's point, conducting of strip or body searches without consent is strictly limited to individuals who present a danger to human life or safety.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Yip asked whether Singapore officers deployed to Malaysia will be able to do their jobs effectively under adequate legal protection.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Bill contains several provisions and safeguards to this effect.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That is made clear in clause 22 of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As mentioned earlier, Malaysia's legislation, which is accessible online, affords protections and immunities to our officers based in Malaysia, similar to what this Bill accords to Malaysian officers based in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To Mr Dennis Tan's point about there being substantive reciprocity in powers and immunities, I will confirm to him that the answer is yes.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Third, the protections and immunities conferred on Malaysian officers in Singapore are conditional on our officers being accorded similar treatment when operating in Malaysia.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Vikram asked about operational measures to prevent smuggling of prohibited or controlled items across the border.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The co-location of CIQ facilities provide convenience for travellers, as many of my colleagues in this House have articulated.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But we have worked hard to ensure that this does not come at the expense of border security.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: First, there will be multiple layers of checks.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Under the Bill, Singapore officers have the powers to conduct selective checks within the designated areas at Bukit Chagar Station.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is on top of the checks that Malaysian officers would have done and conducted on all travellers before they are granted departure clearance at the Bukit Chagar Station.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Second, when these same travellers arrive at Woodlands North Station, they may then also be subject to further selective security checks.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Third, as I have mentioned in my opening speech, Singapore and Malaysia have jointly developed a comprehensive set of standard operational procedures (SOPs) for the purposes of conducting border clearance and security checks in a co-located CIQ arrangement.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These SOPs will ensure smooth coordination between each layer of checks and mitigate the risk of threats slipping through.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And I believe earlier, a Member asked whether we are in contact, whether there will be joint exercises, the answer is, yes, there are.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There are planning exercises as well also ground operational readiness exercises that we will conduct – not just before the start of the operationalisation of the RTS Link, but also subsequently as we continue to run both CIQs and the RTS Link.
